title: How long?
hook: the Psalms let the faithful complain: how long, O Lord? (Psalm 13)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the whirlwind, stars and sea and the hawk heading south. Your line was where were you. Did one wild thing go on without you for a minute? Today we leave Job for the Psalms. Day seven hundred thirteen.

"Are we there yet?" From the back seat, the first time, it's almost cute. By the fourth time, it's a different question. It isn't really asking about the map anymore. It's saying: this is too long, I'm tired, and I don't know if it ends. Grown-ups ask it too, in hospital corridors, in long months out of work, at three in the morning. And the book of Psalms, a book of prayers, keeps that question right inside it.
screen: `ARE WE THERE YET?` → `BY THE FOURTH TIME, A DIFFERENT QUESTION.` → `THE PSALMS KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: First, four times. Psalm thirteen opens: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" And the next verse keeps going: "How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?" Count them. How long, four times, in two verses. It's the back seat, at the fourth asking. Second, for ever? Tucked into the first line is the fear underneath the question. Not just how long, but: is this forever? Has God forgotten me for good? The psalm says that out loud, to God, in a prayer. Third, a complaint in the prayer book. This isn't a private diary that slipped in by mistake. The psalm sits in the book of prayers that Jews and Christians both pray. Its heading gives it to the chief musician, as a psalm of David. Complaint, here, is part of worship. In this prayer a faithful voice says to God: are you hiding, and how long? Fourth, the turn. Then, near the end, the psalm turns: "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation." And the last line: "I will sing unto the LORD, because he hath dealt bountifully with me." Now look closely. The psalm never says the trouble ended. The enemy isn't said to have left. The sorrow isn't said to be gone. The turn to trust comes inside the waiting, not after it. Some readers hear that as the heart of the psalm: the how long and the but I have trusted, side by side, in one short prayer.
screen: `HOW LONG, FOUR TIMES.` · `FOR EVER?` · `A COMPLAINT IN THE PRAYER BOOK.` · `THE TURN COMES INSIDE THE WAITING.` · then, large: `HOW LONG.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath be slow. Find one thing in your life that's taking too long. A healing, an answer, a change, a person coming round. Now form your own how long, one honest sentence, starting with those two words. If there's paper nearby, write it down; if not, write it in your head, word by word. Read it back once. Then leave it on the page, unanswered. No need to add a happy ending. The bell holds the time.
How long?: the question Psalm thirteen asks four times, a faithful person's complaint kept right inside the book of prayers. Today's word.
Your line: but I have trusted. Today, when some waiting wears on you, say how long once, honestly, under your breath, and notice what exactly you're waiting for. Day seven hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray the Psalms, alone and together; psalms of complaint like Psalm 13 are part of that prayer, and some people pray them in times of illness, grief or long waiting.

pairs: asked four times in two verses

myth: the psalm says the trouble ended before the singer turned to trust
it never says the trouble ended; the turn comes inside the waiting.
Psalm 13 asks how long four times
twice in verse one, twice in verse two.
complaining to God has no place in the book of Psalms
Psalm 13 opens with how long wilt thou forget me, O LORD?

fork.setup: you're praying Psalm 13. you've asked how long, four times, and nothing has changed yet. how does the psalm go on?
options: it waits until the enemy is gone, then gives thanks
it turns: but I have trusted in thy mercy
fork.reveal: the psalm turns to trust and song without saying the trouble has ended.

original.note: Hebrew: how long, the words that open Psalm 13.

trapdoor: what you thought: a person of faith isn't supposed to complain to God.
what it means: Psalm 13 asks how long, four times, and keeps the complaint inside a prayer.
what a scholar hears: the psalm moves from complaint (13:1–2) to request (13:3–4) to trust and song (13:5–6), a shape some readers call a psalm of lament.

notes: Editor: 'the faithful are allowed to say: where are you' (a narrator ruling, and words not in the psalm) changed to what the psalm itself asks; stock 'here's what's worth noticing' cut; practice now writes the how long (as the index asks) instead of repeating the 'if you pray, say it to God; if not, say it to...' pattern used in days 711 and 714.
The count 'four times' is taken directly from the KJV text of 13:1–2 (How long ×2, how long ×2); confirm it holds in the Hebrew (עַד־אָנָה ×4).
The heading 'To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David' is paraphrased; in the Hebrew it is verse 1, so verse numbers differ between Hebrew and English Bibles.
Original: עַד־אָנָה with pronunciation ahd-ah-NAH; confirm.
